title: Parmanand: hear, then do
hook: what use is hearing holy stories if devotion doesn't follow (Sarang, Parmanand, ang 1253)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramanand: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love? Your line was colored at home. Did you find a holy place right where you already were? Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

A cookbook on the nightstand, its pages soft from reading in bed. Every recipe known by heart. The oven has never been switched on. Reading about bread is a real pleasure. It just doesn't feed anybody. In Raag Sarang, on Ang 1253 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Parmanand turns to someone who has heard every holy story there is, and asks a blunt question: so what did all that listening do?
screen: `A COOKBOOK READ IN BED.` → `THE OVEN NEVER ON.` → `WHAT DID THE LISTENING DO?`

segments.voice: Parmanand is one of the Bhagats, the devotees outside the line of the Gurus whose words sit in the Granth. The Granth tells us almost nothing about his life. What it keeps is his hymn. It opens, in paraphrase: man, what have you gained by hearing the Puranas? Steady devotion never rose up in you, and you gave nothing to the hungry. The Puranas are old books of sacred stories, gods and kings and devotees, read aloud and loved. Parmanand isn't sneering at the stories. He's looking at the listener who walks away from them unchanged. Then he names what didn't move. In paraphrase again: lust and anger and greed are still there, and the mouth still hasn't stopped speaking ill of others. The stories went in at the ears and stopped. Now look at the test he uses. Not how many stories you know. Not how beautifully you can retell them. Two plain questions. Did devotion grow? And did the hungry get fed? A heart turned toward God, and a hand turned toward the person in front of you. In this hymn the two are named side by side, and the listener has neither. Parmanand says it from his own corner, in his own voice, and the Granth keeps it. Which is a little awkward for a lesson like this one, since a lesson is also something heard. A story heard is a seed in a pocket. Parmanand's question is whether it ever goes into the ground.
screen: `WHAT DID HEARING THE PURANAS GAIN YOU?` · `NOT THE STORIES: THE UNCHANGED LISTENER.` · `TWO TESTS: DEVOTION, AND THE HUNGRY FED.` · `A SEED IN A POCKET.` · then, large: `HEAR, THEN DO.`

segments.voice: The practice: act on one story. In the sit, bring back one story you've heard on this path lately. Sain the barber offering his work. Pipa finding the temple in the body. Ramanand at home in a house colored with love. Pick one. Then ask what it would look like as a single thing done today, small enough to really happen. A meal shared. A sharp word left unsaid. Choose it, and let it settle until it feels like a plan instead of a wish. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Parmanand. A Bhagat whose hymn in Raag Sarang asks what the hearing was for, if devotion never grew and the hungry went unfed.
Your line: hear, then do. Today, take one thing you heard, from a lesson, a friend or a page, and do it before dark. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Parmanand's hymn in Raag Sarang is sung in kirtan like other Gurbani, and Sikhs read it as a call to let what is heard in the gurdwara change how they live and give.

options: how many more stories do you know?

fork.reveal: he asks what was gained: did devotion grow, did the hungry get fed? the hearing isn't the problem; staying unchanged is.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn against listening to religious stories.
what it means: hearing is only the start; Parmanand asks for devotion that grows and a hand that feeds the hungry.
what a scholar hears: a Bhagat's question about the Puranas, kept in the Granth in his own voice, with devotion and feeding the hungry as the two tests.
